job: Fresh graduate in business, finance and accounting
name: Tomas Weber

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. Tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a junior auditor at Harlow and Pike, a small firm in Leicester with about 30 staff. Most days I'm at a client's office or at my desk, ticking invoices against bank statements and filling in working papers. I'm paid for 37 hours but I'm usually out at half six. I share a damp three-bed flat with two mates, and most of my pay goes on rent and loan payments.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say it's mostly hype and the firm should spend on training people, not on software licences. Online I'd post that every new tool gets sold as the end of work and then the rent is still due. I wouldn't argue with the partners about it, though.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'm not calm even then, because the tick-and-tie work I do all day is exactly what these small tools nibble at. If the firm saves a few hours on each audit, they just won't replace the next person who leaves. I have less than a month of rent and bills saved, and my loan is more than two years of my take-home pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my head down and learn the firm's audit software properly, because the seniors rate people who know it. I'd put 80 a month into a savings pot, which is all I can spare, and keep going to my evening exam classes. I'd keep paying my union dues too, small as they are.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tense, mostly. Not terrified, because the job exists today. I check my payslip and my loan balance the way some people check the weather.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned a union. Is there one at Harlow and Pike?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, it's a national finance workers' union that I joined myself. Nobody else at the firm is in it, which is a bit lonely. I'd like to start the conversation in the office, but a trainee asking for a meeting about pay isn't safe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What gets cut first if money gets tighter?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Going out first, then the train to see my sister. I won't touch the exam fees, because without the qualification I'm stuck on a trainee wage for good. I'd sooner eat pasta for a month than drop the course.

say: I'd say **hype** is the right word and the firm should invest in people, not licences.
I'd say the tools are small and the **rent** is still due.
think: The tick-and-tie work that fills my day is what small tools **nibble** at first.
Fewer **replacements** when people leave is how it would reach me, quietly.
My **debt** is over two years of take-home pay, so I can't afford a quiet year.
do: Learn the firm's **audit software** properly so the seniors rate me.
Put **80** a month into savings, the most I can spare.
Keep going to evening **exam classes** for my accountancy qualification.
feel: **Tense** every payday, checking my loan balance like the weather.
S0.quote: I check my payslip and my loan balance the way some people check the weather.
fieldNote: His **debt** and thin savings make even a quiet scenario stressful.
He's lonely as the only union member at the firm, and says so plainly.
Protects his exam fees above everything, seeing the qualification as his only route up.

steps.text: Learn the firm's audit software properly this winter
Put 80 a month into a savings pot
Skip nights out and train trips to my sister

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it out loud: if software does the checking, the firm owes the juniors real training in judgement, not just fewer hours. I'd say it to colleagues first and put it in the union branch chat. The big firms are the ones cashing in, and they'll pass the bill to people like me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd expect to be in the group that gets squeezed. My job is the checking, and checking is the first thing that goes to software. The firm hired two graduates this year and I'd guess it hires none next year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask a partner, Mr Pike, to put me on the client-facing work, where people still want a person in the room. I'd cut my spending to the bone and put every spare bit into the savings pot. I'd also start emailing other firms in the region, even though it's a small market.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried and a bit angry. I did everything right: top of the class, two internships, and now the ladder's rungs are being sawn off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at Harlow and Pike would you worry about first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The two interns who sit next to me, and the clerks in the back office who've been there 15 years. They don't have a qualification to fall back on. If the juniors go, they'd be the next ones out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd talk to the partners. What would you actually say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that a firm making money from software that does the work of juniors should pay into something for the people it stops hiring. I know the partners would just roll their eyes. But I'd rather say it once and be called difficult than say nothing.

say: I'd say the firm owes juniors **real training** if software does the checking.
I'd say the big firms are **cashing in** and passing the bill down.
think: Checking is my job and the first thing software takes, so I'll likely be **squeezed**.
The firm hired two graduates this year and I'd guess **none** next year.
do: Ask Mr Pike (a partner) to put me on **client-facing** work.
Cut spending to the bone and save **every spare bit**.
Email other firms in the region, even though the **market** is small.
feel: **Angry** and worried: I did everything right and the ladder's rungs are being sawn off.
S1.quote: I did everything right: top of the class, two internships, and now the ladder's rungs are being sawn off.
fieldNote: He blames **big firms** and owners, not the tools themselves.
Anger is covering real fear; he expects to be one of the first to be cut.
He'd speak up once even knowing the partners would roll their eyes.

steps.text: Ask a partner to move me onto client-facing work

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the world has gone past the point where one firm can fix this, and the government has to step in with real support. I'd be on every march and petition I could get to. Saying it quietly in the office wouldn't be enough.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I think my whole degree could be worth very little by 2028. Auditing is thinking work, on screens, with rules, which is exactly what this AGI does better. I've got a loan I can't wipe, no family money, and I don't have a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd freeze for a week and then probably do everything badly. I'd try to cram 6 months of rent into savings, but I can't see how with my pay. I'd go to the union and ask what they're demanding, and I'd phone my sister every night.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick, to be honest. I feel like I've missed the last bus home in a town I don't know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Two years is very short. What do you do the day you hear it's arrived?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd leave work and sit in the car park for ten minutes, I think. Then I'd go back in and finish my working papers, because I wouldn't know what else to do. It's the sort of day where you do the next small task and try not to look up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who do you turn to, if anyone?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My sister Leila, who is a care assistant, and the union. Not the firm. The partners would be looking after their own pensions, I'd imagine. I'd be asking the state for help, and I'd want to be one of many asking so we couldn't be ignored.

say: I'd say **one firm** can't fix this and the government must step in with real support.
I'd join every **march** and petition I could get to.
think: My degree could be worth **very little** by 2028, because auditing is rules on a screen.
I have a loan I can't wipe, no family money and **no plan**.
do: Try to cram **6 months** of rent into savings, though I can't see how.
Ask the **union** what it's demanding and join in.
Phone my sister **every night** for support.
feel: **Sick**, like missing the last bus home in a town I don't know.
S2.quote: I feel like I've missed the last bus home in a town I don't know.
fieldNote: He has **no plan** and says so; debt and no family help leave no room to move.
He turns to the union and his sister, not the firm, trusting numbers over partners.
Freezing first, then small tasks, shows how resistant he is to fast change.

steps.text: Try to build 6 months of rent in savings
Ask the union what it's demanding and join in
Join marches and petitions for public support
Phone my sister every night for support

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is long enough for the government to do something if people push hard. I'd say it at the branch meeting and online. I'd say we need a retraining guarantee and a shorter working week, not a lecture about adapting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years feels like a reprieve I'm scared to waste. I'd have the qualification by then, maybe a manager's role at one of the few firms still hiring. But I know that thinking AI arrives at that date regardless, and I'm not sure my skills outlast it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the accountancy exams, because that's the one thing I've paid for. I'd save 150 a month if I get a raise. I'd also look at moving to the capital where there's more work, though it would mean rent I can't pay yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit more breathing room, but it's a slow dread. Five years is enough to get my hopes up and then lose them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What changes for you with five years instead of two?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With two years I'd be freezing. With five I can at least study something for a year, perhaps a public-sector accounting course, since councils and charities may keep humans longer. That's the only difference. The debt is still there either way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell a younger cousin about to start the same degree?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my cousin Daniel not to study accounting for the money, and to study it only if he likes the puzzle of it. I'd say get a trade or a public-sector route if he can. The version I'd want him to hear is that nobody can promise him a ladder to climb.

say: I'd say five years is long enough if people **push hard** for a retraining guarantee.
I'd say we need a **shorter week**, not a lecture about adapting.
think: Five years is a **reprieve** I'm scared to waste.
Thinking AI arrives at that date regardless, and I'm not sure my skills **outlast** it.
do: Finish the accountancy **exams**, the one thing I've paid for.
Save **150** a month if I get a raise.
Look at **public-sector** accounting study, where humans may stay longer.
feel: A bit more **breathing room**, but a slow dread underneath.
S3.quote: I'd tell my cousin Daniel not to study accounting for the money, and to study it only if he likes the puzzle of it.
fieldNote: Five years gives him a real **plan**: finish exams, then try public-sector work.
He still wants collective answers: a guarantee of retraining and a shorter week.
His advice to his cousin shows how much trust in the degree has been lost.

steps.text: Finish the accountancy exams on schedule
Save 150 a month once I get a raise
Study public-sector accounting in my second year
Press for a retraining guarantee through the union

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's the job of governments and big firms to use ten years well, and that they won't unless we make them. I'd say that to anyone who'd listen. Ten years is exactly how long it takes to organise people properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm calmer, because by 2036 I'd be 32 and could have paid off a chunk of the debt. But I know I'd be the person who stayed in accounting too long. A decade is enough to get complacent and then be 33 with nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the qualification and move up to senior auditor. I'd put aside at least 200 a month and aim to clear half my loan in five years. I'd help set up a small union branch at the firm, because ten years is enough time to build something that protects people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calmer than the others but still careful. Time helps, but my mum used to say that a long road is still a road you have to walk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Ten years is a long runway. Does it feel like one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels like a runway only if the first few years go well. If I'm still on trainee money in two years, ten years is just a slower way of watching it happen. The loan interest doesn't wait.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want your employer to do over those ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want a proper training budget, paid study time and a promise that nobody gets let go the month a tool is switched on. Notice periods, retraining, an honest plan on the wall. If they won't promise it, that tells me what they think of us.

say: I'd say governments and big firms must use the **ten years** well and we must make them.
I'd say a decade is how long it takes to **organise** people properly.
think: By 2036 I'd be 32 and could have cleared a chunk of the **debt**.
A decade is enough to get **complacent** and end up with nothing at 33.
do: Finish my qualification and move up to **senior auditor**.
Put aside **200** a month to clear half my loan in five years.
Help set up a small **union branch** at the firm.
feel: **Calmer** than in the faster pictures, but careful.
S4.quote: A long road is still a road you have to walk.
fieldNote: Ten years turns his worry into **organising**: a union branch and a savings target.
He fears complacency, which fits a man who prefers the familiar.
Interest on the loan keeps the calm partial; money, not time, is his real limit.

steps.text: Pass the final exams and apply for senior auditor
Save 200 a month to clear half the loan

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one worries me most. I've got debt, no family money and a job that's mostly checking, so I'd have no time and no cushion. What would help is a proper income guarantee, retraining that's paid for, and employers who say in writing that they won't let people go overnight.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that people my age are told to be flexible, when the ones who owe the most have the least room to move. I'm not asking for charity. I'm asking for a ladder that's still there when I get to the top of it.

headlineQuote: I'm not asking for charity. I'm asking for a ladder that's still there when I get to the top of it.
portrait: Tomas is a **22-year-old** junior auditor in Leicester on a trainee contract, with heavy student debt and almost no savings.
He's progressive and distrusts big firms, so he wants **collective** answers: unions, regulation and public support.
He prefers the familiar and has never used AI tools, which leaves him with little room to move if the job shrinks.
His mood climbs from anxious to **panicked** in the two-year world and eases only a little when he has ten years.
biggestWorry: The **two-year** picture, because he'd have debt, no family money and no time to build a cushion.
whatWouldHelp: A **paid** retraining route and an income guarantee, plus employers who promise in writing not to cut jobs overnight.
